original_target.title: Can a three-dimensional ancient Ricci flow have spatially unbounded curvature?

full_original_statement:
Does there exist a connected smooth noncompact three-manifold $`M`$, without boundary, and a smooth family of complete Riemannian metrics $`g(t)`$, $`t\in(-\infty,0)`$, satisfying
```math
\partial_t g(t)=-2\mathrm{Ric}_{g(t)},\qquad
K_{g(t)}(\sigma)\ge0
```

for every tangent two-plane $`\sigma`$ and every $`t<0`$, such that for some interior time $`t_0<0`$,
```math
\sup_{p\in M}\left|\mathrm{Rm}_{g(t_0)}(p)\right|_{g(t_0)}=\infty?
```


Here completeness is required at every time. Unboundedness refers to the spatial supremum at a fixed time, rather than curvature growth as time approaches an endpoint. No noncollapsing, symmetry or uniform curvature-pinching hypothesis is imposed.

sources.scope_comparison: The unbounded example is explicitly immortal t>=0, not defined over an infinite backward interval, and Remark8.5(b) distinguishes the ancient question. Yokota's actual theorem rules out such examples under uniform Ric>=rho scal g with rho>0, stronger than mere sectional nonnegativity. Ancient kappa-solution classification includes bounded-curvature and noncollapsing assumptions; dropping them is the target. Two-dimensional boundary constructions and Kähler shrinker results also have different dimensions or hypotheses. No exact complete announcement located.
